questions.topic: Storage-Compute Separation and the Columnar Engine
questions.question: In BigQuery's architecture, what is a slot?
options: A reserved partition of Colossus storage dedicated to one project's table data
A unit of compute capacity, roughly a virtual CPU with memory, rented to a query for its duration
A network channel between the storage plane and compute plane assigned per table
A scheduling window during which a project is permitted to submit query jobs

questions.topic: Storage-Compute Separation and the Columnar Engine
questions.question: Why does selecting 2 columns from a 32-column table scan far fewer bytes than selecting all columns?
options: Because the engine caches previously queried columns and serves repeats from memory
Because the planner samples a subset of rows first and extrapolates the full result
Because unselected columns are stored compressed and are skipped only after decompression
Because columnar storage keeps each column's values contiguous, so only referenced columns are read

questions.topic: Storage-Compute Separation and the Columnar Engine
questions.question: A nightly ETL pipeline and an analyst's exploratory queries hit the same BigQuery tables at the same time. What property of the architecture prevents them from corrupting or blocking each other's data access?
options: Storage and compute are separate planes, so both workloads read shared storage with independent compute
Each table keeps one writer lock, so the pipeline and the analyst take turns executing
The analyst's queries run on read replicas that are refreshed after the pipeline commits
The engine copies each queried table into per-user scratch space before execution begins

questions.topic: Storage-Compute Separation and the Columnar Engine
questions.question: A GROUP BY query over 10 billion events runs slowly even after slots are doubled, and one worker processes far longer than the rest. What is the likely cause?
options: The table lacks indexes, so every worker must scan the entire dataset repeatedly
The shuffle tier ran out of quota, forcing all workers to serialize their output
A heavily skewed grouping key concentrated one shuffle partition on a single worker
The query exceeded the two-stage limit, so extra stages executed without parallelism

questions.topic: Storage-Compute Separation and the Columnar Engine
questions.question: A team plans to use BigQuery as the backend for an app that updates individual user rows hundreds of times per second. Why is this architecturally wrong?
options: BigQuery tables become read-only once they exceed their first billion rows
BigQuery cannot express UPDATE statements, so rows can never be modified
Each DML statement runs as a distributed job rather than an indexed row write, so frequent single-row updates are slow and costly
Each update triggers a full table re-cluster, locking out reads until it completes

questions.topic: Storage-Compute Separation and the Columnar Engine
questions.question: Which consequence follows directly from BigQuery separating storage from compute?
options: Petabytes can sit in storage costing nothing for compute until they are actually queried
Data must be reloaded into compute nodes whenever a new reservation is created
Storage throughput drops whenever many slots are active, since they share machines
Tables must be pre-sized for compute capacity before any data can be loaded

questions.topic: Partitioning and Clustering in BigQuery
questions.question: What does partition pruning do?
options: It deletes partitions that have passed their configured expiration age
It merges small partitions into larger ones to reduce metadata overhead
It re-sorts rows within each partition so block metadata stays accurate
It eliminates entire partitions from a scan at planning time based on the filter

questions.topic: Partitioning and Clustering in BigQuery
questions.question: How does clustering reduce the bytes a query reads?
options: By compressing cluster columns with a dictionary shared across the whole table
By sorting data into blocks whose min/max metadata lets non-matching blocks be skipped
By storing cluster columns in a separate index table consulted before the scan
By caching the most frequently filtered column values in the shuffle tier

questions.topic: Partitioning and Clustering in BigQuery
questions.question: A 730 GB events table is partitioned by day across two years. A dashboard filters to the last 7 days. Roughly what does the query scan?
options: About 365 GB, since pruning eliminates at most half of a table's partitions
About 730 GB, since partitioning affects storage layout but not scan volume
About 7 GB, since pruning skips all but the seven matching daily partitions
About 73 GB, since pruning works at monthly rather than daily granularity

questions.topic: Partitioning and Clustering in BigQuery
questions.question: Every query against a multi-tenant retrieval corpus filters on `tenant_id`, a column with 50,000 distinct values. Which physical design serves this filter best?
options: Partition the table by `tenant_id` so each tenant's rows form their own partition
Cluster the table with `tenant_id` as the first clustering column
Shard the corpus into 50,000 separate tables, one per tenant identifier
Add `require_partition_filter` so queries must always name a tenant

questions.topic: Partitioning and Clustering in BigQuery
questions.question: A query filters a date-partitioned table with `WHERE partition_date = other_table.max_date` via a join, yet scans the entire table. Why did pruning fail?
options: The filter value is not resolvable at planning time, and pruning happens before execution
The partition column was compared with equality, and pruning requires range predicates
The table also has clustering columns, which override partition pruning when present
The join forced a shuffle, and shuffled tables always bypass the pruning step

questions.topic: Partitioning and Clustering in BigQuery
questions.question: A table is clustered by (`customer_id`, `event_type`). Which query benefits least from block pruning?
options: A query filtering on `customer_id` alone with an equality predicate
A query filtering on both `customer_id` and `event_type` together
A query filtering on `customer_id` with an IN list of a few values
A query filtering on `event_type` alone without any customer predicate

questions.topic: Editions, Reservations, and Slot Autoscaling
questions.question: What is a reservation in BigQuery's capacity model?
options: A prepaid discount contract covering a fixed number of on-demand queries
A quota on the maximum bytes a project may scan in one billing month
A scheduled maintenance window during which slots are upgraded per project
A named pool of slots created centrally and assigned to projects, folders, or an org

questions.topic: Editions, Reservations, and Slot Autoscaling
questions.question: In an autoscaling reservation, what does the baseline represent?
options: The minimum queue depth required before any autoscaled slots are added
The slots that are always allocated and billed, with autoscaling adding more up to the max
The average slot usage measured over the previous month of workloads
The number of slots shared out to other reservations while the owner is idle

questions.topic: Editions, Reservations, and Slot Autoscaling
questions.question: Data scientists' ad-hoc queries keep slowing the SLA-bound nightly ETL under a single shared reservation. What is the standard fix?
options: Raise the shared reservation's max so autoscaling absorbs everyone's peak together
Move the data scientists to a different region so their queries use separate capacity
Create separate reservations per workload and assign the projects accordingly
Switch the ETL project to on-demand pricing so it no longer competes for slots

questions.topic: Editions, Reservations, and Slot Autoscaling
questions.question: A team sets baseline 0 and max 400 on their reservation. What behavior should they expect?
options: Zero cost at idle, with slots scaling up on demand and billed per second while provisioned
Zero cost at idle, but queries fail until an administrator manually allocates slots
Constant billing for 400 slots, since the max determines the reservation's charge
Constant billing for 200 slots, since billing uses the midpoint of baseline and max

questions.topic: Editions, Reservations, and Slot Autoscaling
questions.question: An organization needs multi-region disaster recovery for BigQuery workloads plus the strongest compliance controls. Which Edition tier is the match?
options: Standard, since disaster recovery is included in every Edition tier
Enterprise Plus, since it adds the compliance and cross-region DR ceiling
Enterprise, since it is the designated production tier for all workloads
Any tier, provided a three-year slot commitment is attached to it

questions.topic: Editions, Reservations, and Slot Autoscaling
questions.question: How should an expert set the baseline for a reservation with variable but sustained daytime load?
options: At zero always, because autoscaled slots are cheaper per hour than baseline slots
At the P99 of usage, because latency consistency outweighs all idle-slot cost
At the licensed maximum, because idle slots are shared and thus never wasted
Near the P50 of sustained usage, letting autoscaling absorb the peaks above it

questions.topic: On-Demand vs Capacity Pricing: Estimating Cost
questions.question: What does on-demand BigQuery pricing bill for?
options: The wall-clock duration each query holds its transient slot allocation
The rows returned to the client after all filters and limits are applied
The bytes processed from the referenced columns in the data actually read
The number of query jobs submitted by the project in the billing month

questions.topic: On-Demand vs Capacity Pricing: Estimating Cost
questions.question: What does a dry run of a query return?
options: The bytes the query would process, computed without executing the query
The rows the query would return, sampled from a fraction of the table
The slot-hours the query would consume under the current reservation
The estimated wall-clock runtime based on similar historical queries

questions.topic: On-Demand vs Capacity Pricing: Estimating Cost
questions.question: An analyst adds `LIMIT 10` to a query on a large unpartitioned table to keep on-demand costs down. What actually happens?
options: The cost drops proportionally, since only ten rows are read from storage
The cost drops only when the table is clustered on the selected columns
The query is rejected, since LIMIT requires a partition filter to execute
The cost is unchanged, since the full scan happens before the limit applies

questions.topic: On-Demand vs Capacity Pricing: Estimating Cost
questions.question: A query selects 4 of 40 equal-width columns from a 2 TB table, filtered to 30 of 365 daily partitions. Roughly what does it process on-demand?
options: About 200 GB, since column selection reduces the scan but date filters do not
About 16 GB, since bytes scale by the column fraction times the partition fraction
About 2 TB, since on-demand billing always charges the full size of the table
About 160 GB, since partition pruning applies but column pruning does not

questions.topic: On-Demand vs Capacity Pricing: Estimating Cost
questions.question: A finance team demands a hard guarantee that no single ad-hoc query can produce a surprise multi-thousand-dollar charge under on-demand pricing. Which control delivers that guarantee?
options: Setting `maximum_bytes_billed` so any query exceeding the cap fails instead of billing
Enabling clustering on all large tables so estimates become strict upper bounds
Reviewing `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS` weekly so expensive queries are flagged early
Granting analysts read access only to views so base tables cannot be scanned

questions.topic: On-Demand vs Capacity Pricing: Estimating Cost
questions.question: An org scans about 400 TiB per month with spiky, unpredictable usage. Another org scans about 5 PiB per month, steadily, and wants flat predictable spend. Which pricing pairing is right?
options: Capacity for the first org and on-demand for the second, since spiky loads need reserved headroom
On-demand for both orgs, since per-byte billing is always cheaper than slot billing
On-demand for the first org and capacity for the second, since sustained heavy volume favors slots
Capacity for both orgs, since reservations are required once monthly scans pass one TiB
